TREC RAG 2026

Single-pass and multi-stage answer generation, traced through one request

Nidhin Pattaniyil · Tanwir Zaman · Semih Yagli — NP Labs

2026-11-16

What the track asks

The task

119 long-form requests, each a paragraph of context and several questions

1,024 words allowed in the answer, at most

every statement has to cite the documents it came from

One variable in this talk: given identical evidence, does drafting once differ from drafting, auditing and revising? Same retrieval, same passages.

This is about how the approach works, not a claim that it is novel. Every number shown is the organizers’ own, from the score files they released.

The whole approach

How it works

Plan once, search wide, narrow to evidence, then write twice. The rest of this talk walks the left-to-right path with one real request.

The request we will follow

The example · rag2026-18 · one of the 119

Six weeks of housing for a family of three — without booking something illegal or unreliable.

Our family of three may need furnished temporary housing in New York City for about six weeks while our apartment is repaired.

… Airbnb/Vrbo, an extended-stay hotel, corporate housing, or a short sublet?

… how should we compare the real costs, safety, cancellation risk, space, location, and day-to-day practicality,

… especially with a child and remote work needs?

Eight things asked at once. Hold on to the two bold facts — they sit in different sentences, and only one of the two answers ever joins them.

Planning: how it works

How it works

Planning only — it never sees a document and is never called again. Deliberately not an agentic loop. At most 25 searches per topic.

The prompt that does the planning

How it works · verbatim

Plan retrieval over a very large passage collection using only the
supplied official topic narrative. Do not answer the topic. Return
only the schema-constrained JSON plan.

Rules:
1. Generate one to eight concise subnarratives that together preserve
   the narrative's requested subjects, relations, comparisons,
   constraints, and uncertainty.
2. Give each subnarrative one to three plain BM25 queries. Queries
   must be useful lexical alternatives, not answers, and must not
   contain query operators or field syntax.
3. Use only the supplied narrative.

The whole planning instruction, copied from the code. “Do not answer the topic” does the heavy lifting — the planner proposes searches, never findings.

Planning: this request

The example · 8 subnarratives × 2 queries = 16 searches for this one request

What options exist? furnished temporary housing New York City family three six weeks short term furnished rental NYC family child
How do the four types compare? Airbnb vs extended stay hotel vs corporate housing vs sublet comparison short term rental types NYC family advantages disadvantages
Which listings are illegal? illegal short term rental NYC avoid scams unreliable temporary housing New York City red flags
What does it really cost? real cost comparison short term rental NYC fees taxes hidden costs temporary housing New York City
Is it safe for a child? safety family short term rental New York City neighborhood child safe temporary housing NYC
What if we cancel? cancellation policy short term rental NYC flexible cancellation temporary housing New York City
Is there room to work? space family short term rental NYC one bedroom temporary housing space child remote work New York City
Is the location practical? location convenience short term rental NYC public transit temporary housing near work school New York City

Click any subnarrative to see the actual queries sent for it. Plain keywords, no operators. This request pushed the planner to its ceiling of eight.

Searching: how it works

How it works

These are ceilings, not yields. Every number is a configured per-query cap, not a count of what actually came back.

Evidence and nuggets: how it works

How it works

Both writers then get one frozen package: the request, the exact evidence, the nuggets, and the citation IDs they are allowed to use. Nothing else.

Evidence and nuggets: this request

The example · facet f001, legality and reliability

Passages — the authority Exact retrieved text, plus the citation IDs this answer is allowed to use.

Every claim has to land on one of these.

Nuggets — advisory hints n092 NYC defines a short-term rental as fewer than 30 consecutive days

n094 NYC has cracked down on illegal rentals, including raids and fines

These are our own hints, not the organizers’ gold nuggets — and n092 is a trap. The family needs six weeks, which is longer than 30 days, so the definition settles nothing on its own.

Two writers: how it works

How it works

Sol writes both. Multi-stage adds Luna as planner, auditor and screener — and starts from the evidence, not from the single-pass answer. If revision fails the validated draft stands, so the extra stages can only add.

What Luna keeps, and what she throws out

How it works · the screening gate

Five gates, all must pass Luna returns only booleans — support, atomicity, materiality, redundancy, replacement safety.

Local code applies an edit only when all five are true. The screen never rewrites prose itself.

Dev topic Edits kept
233 1 of 4
300 3 of 3
499 4 of 5

On topic 499 the screen rejected a replacement that would have erased a distinct argument. These are three development topics, not the 119 — the competition run kept no per-topic audit log.

Two writers: this request

The example · same sealed evidence, two strategies

Single-pass 22 statements · 504 words

Multi-stage 38 statements · 800 words

Both spotted the 30-day trap. Single-pass noted six weeks exceeds it; multi-stage added that the definition alone does not establish whether a particular six-week sublet is lawful.

The difference you can see

The example · one difference you can read

Single-pass · 22 statements Covers legality, cost, safety, space, location.

The word “lead” never appears.

Multi-stage · statement 24 “If the apartment repairs involve lead hazards, ask whether the temporary unit is appropriate for a child and has been made lead-safe.”

The request never says “lead.” It says the apartment is being repaired, and separately that there is a child. One writer joined those two facts. That is a difference you can read — not a claim about which nugget the scoring counted.

What the organizers said about it

The example · NIST Batch 2, human-written nuggets

rag2026-18 Single-pass Multi-stage Field median
Vital nuggets supported 0.857 1.000 0.857
All nuggets supported 0.929 1.000 0.786
Assessor battles fought 10 6 —
… answer preferred 7 6 —
… answer rejected 3 0 —

Each run is judged against other teams’ answers, not against the other one of ours. The battle counts are separate samples, so they do not say a human ever chose between these two. This is also one of 42 scored topics.

When the two measures disagree

A different topic · rag2026-13, a founder scaling a startup

rag2026-13 Single-pass Multi-stage
All nuggets supported 1.000 0.857
Assessor battles fought 10 12
… answer preferred 5 8

The automated rubric scored single-pass higher. The human assessors preferred multi-stage in 8 of its 12 battles, against 5 of single-pass’s 10. The two measures rank our runs the opposite way round.

The rubric items were not released, so we cannot name what was credited or missed — only that the two measures disagree here.

Overall: 42 scored topics

Across everything NIST scored

26 topics where multi-stage supported more nuggets

15 topics where the two tied exactly

1 topic where single-pass did better

62.9% of multi-stage’s 399 assessor battles were won

45.0% of single-pass’s 422 battles were won

Multi-stage costs several extra model calls per topic for this. Nothing here is a claim that it is novel — only that the extra passes did something visible.

A word on the retrieval side

The other submission

All three Retrieval runs differ only in ordering and scored identically, per topic included. This measures what we selected; it says nothing about which ordering puts useful documents first.

What I would and would not claim from this

Limits

Supported With evidence held fixed, multi-stage got higher coverage and a better assessor record, on every collection.

Not supported Which stage caused it — planning, auditing, revision, model mix and length all moved together.

That length explains it. Multi-stage wrote 531–1,011 words against 203–749.

Better grounding. A separate RAGDoll check favoured single-pass, 0.757 against 0.653.

The organizer gains should not be read as better grounding. Coverage and citation support are different questions, and here they point different ways.
